title: Ecological and social cues orchestrate concerted courtship in Drosophila
abstract:
In Drosophila erecta, food odours initiate male sexual arousal, which is subsequently reinforced by the visual motion of other courting flies, creating a multisensory mechanism that synchronizes courtship in groups when conditions are favourable for reproduction. 
 Mating decisions are often attributed to the sensory signalling between prospective sexual partners. Yet these interactions are also shaped by the broader environmental context in which they unfold, to appropriately align sexual arousal with reproductive opportunities1–6. Here we show that in Drosophila erecta mating is strictly contingent on the ecological and social environment generated as flies densely aggregate in groups on a food patch. We find that food volatiles directly promote male sexual arousal, triggering individuals to sample and pursue potential mates, giving rise to dynamic interactions across the group. The ensuing visual motion transforms each male’s visual field, which in turn further amplifies his arousal, generating a multisensory feedback loop that coordinately promotes courtship across individuals. D. erecta’s strict dependence on environmental cues appears latent in related species, such as Drosophila melanogaster, where food odour can promote arousal7 but is dispensable for vigorous courtship. Comparative circuit analyses show that species-specific thresholds for sexual arousal reflect variation in how olfactory input modulates conserved nodes controlling courtship drive, rendering food volatiles a strict sensory gate only in D. erecta. Together, our findings highlight how environmental cues not directly tied to sexual signalling can profoundly influence reproductive behaviour and reorganize the social landscape to ensure mating occurs in contexts where reproductive opportunities are abundant. In Drosophila erecta, food odours initiate male sexual arousal, which is subsequently reinforced by the visual motion of other courting flies, creating a multisensory mechanism that synchronizes courtship in groups when conditions are favourable for reproduction.

title: An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations
abstract:
AutoDNA is an artificial intelligence (AI)-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments, realizing the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework. 
 Developing artificial intelligence (AI)-native experimental laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention represents a long-standing goal. Although autonomous experimental systems are emerging1–4, especially in chemical and materials science, they remain largely confined to domains with singular objectives, well-defined workflows and simple instrumentation. This limitation may reflect an ‘add-on’ architecture that uses AI as a task-specific tool rather than providing it with a global understanding of experiments, especially under engineering-oriented circumstances. Here we present AutoDNA, an AI-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments. Through the co-design of models, experiments and instruments, AutoDNA realizes the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework. The system autonomously orchestrates over 20 types of instruments across more than 11,000 steps to execute core nucleic acid operations including synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing, while human intervention is limited to hardware maintenance tasks, such as reagent and labware replenishment. Across four representative applications, AutoDNA matched expert-optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis yields, accelerated concurrent protocol execution by 3.2-fold, completed an end-to-end DNA data storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content, and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation. AutoDNA establishes a blueprint towards science-as-a-service, accelerating biological discovery and advancing various applications in synthetic biology and information storage. AutoDNA is an artificial intelligence (AI)-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments, realizing the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework.

title: Multimodal X-ray imaging reveals hierarchical fibre mechanics
abstract:
The X-ray visualization platform TomoSAXS, demonstrated here on intervertebral spinal discs, can visualize nanoscale to macroscale mechanics in intact biological organs and fibrous materials. 
 Fibrous materials, ranging from connective tissues1–4 to engineered composites5–8, are vital to many biological and man-made systems, optimized to withstand complex in operando or in vivo loading. The load-bearing capacity of intervertebral discs (IVDs) of the spine depends on a hierarchical extracellular matrix, where plywood-like lamellae of collagen fibres in the annulus fibrosus contain nanometre-scale fibrils built from staggered triple-helical monomers4,9,10. How intact IVDs couple fibril-scale mechanics to fibre-scale organization under load remains unresolved. Here we introduce TomoSAXS, a full-field 3D small-angle X-ray scattering tomography that maps fibril-to-fibre mechanics across an intact tissue. We show that intrafibrillar molecular pre-strain (D-period stagger) is lamellar textured and tightly correlated with microscale fibre strain. Pre-strain is inversely related to fibril strain and its variability, consistent with load-sharing through molecular unwinding. Radial strain bridges and high-curvature zones at the annulus fibrosus–nucleus pulposus interfaces emerge as critical regulators of local mechanics. These findings reveal concerted fibril–fibre interactions that sustain mechanical equilibrium in the IVD, preserving elasticity and shape. More broadly, TomoSAXS establishes a platform to visualize nanoscale-to-microscale matrix mechanics across biological and synthetic fibrous materials, with applications in ageing and disease, therapeutic evaluation and the design of bio-based and bio-inspired materials. The X-ray visualization platform TomoSAXS, demonstrated here on intervertebral spinal discs, can visualize nanoscale to macroscale mechanics in intact biological organs and fibrous materials.

title: Towards observing interstitial hydrogen in solution in metal lattices
abstract:
Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, atom probe tomography provides experimental evidence for interstitial hydrogen in solid solution across different FCC phases, consistent with theoretical predictions of hydrogen affinity, revealing hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys. 
 Hydrogen-bearing materials are central to low-carbon energy technologies1, but hydrogen itself is difficult to detect and localize at the nanoscale2–6. This hinders the development of advanced materials with better efficiency. Atom probe tomography (APT) can map hydrogen in three dimensions and at high resolution, yet characterization of dilute, mobile, interstitial hydrogen in metals has remained challenging because of low solubility, the ambiguity owing to hydrogen trapping by structural defects, as well as the artefacts introduced during hydrogen introduction4–6. Here we address whether interstitial hydrogen in solution in materials can be distinguished from defect-trapped hydrogen in APT. Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, together with face-centred cubic (FCC) multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) containing coherent FCC precipitates, we show that deuterium atoms reproducibly concentrate in hydrogen-affinitive phases in a manner consistent with theoretical predictions. We further resolve differences in deuterium content between phases with distinct local chemistries and crystal structures, consistent with their different calculated hydrogen solution energies. These findings demonstrate that APT can move beyond identifying hydrides and solute-decorated defects to examine hydrogen in solid solution, providing new insights into hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys and informing materials design for hydrogen-related applications. Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, atom probe tomography provides experimental evidence for interstitial hydrogen in solid solution across different FCC phases, consistent with theoretical predictions of hydrogen affinity, revealing hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys.

title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
abstract:
Multi-omic analyses of cells from patients with glioblastoma (GB) provide insight into the role of non-genetic cellular plasticity in disease progression, showing that state stability in GB cells is controlled by a network of interacting activators and repressors. 
 Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment1–8, suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear9–13. Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance. Multi-omic analyses of cells from patients with glioblastoma (GB) provide insight into the role of non-genetic cellular plasticity in disease progression, showing that state stability in GB cells is controlled by a network of interacting activators and repressors.

title: Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis
abstract:
A high-throughput CRISPR-interference platform allows the mapping of interactions between essential genes in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, revealing many previously unknown genetic interactions and providing insight into gene function and drug–target relationships that could enable the development of new therapies for tuberculosis. 
 Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis, remains the world’s deadliest pathogen1. Despite intensive study, many of its genes remain uncharacterized, which limits the insight that can be gained into tuberculosis biology and constrains drug development. Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful strategy to define functional relationships between genes by quantifying how the phenotypic effects of combined perturbations deviate from expectations based on single-gene perturbations2,3. Here we develop a dual-sgRNA CRISPR-interference platform that enables high-throughput GI mapping in mycobacteria. We address key technical challenges in library construction and data interpretation by incorporating unique barcodes for each sgRNA pair and implementing a robust statistical pipeline for GI detection. Focusing on essential genes, we generate comprehensive GI maps in the model mycobacterium Mycobacterium smegmatis and the pathogen M. tuberculosis. These maps recapitulate known biology, uncover thousands of previously unrecognized interactions and identify functional connections between essential genes and drug targets. By generating AlphaFold3-based protein–protein interaction predictions4 for all gene pairs in our GI maps, we show that a subset of GIs is likely to reflect underlying physical associations. Validation of selected GIs confirms both novel biological relationships and opportunities for synergistic targeting. Overall, this work establishes a generalizable framework for dual-gene perturbation and defines the architecture of essential-gene networks in mycobacteria, advancing both our understanding of tuberculosis biology and the rational design of combination therapies. A high-throughput CRISPR-interference platform allows the mapping of interactions between essential genes in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, revealing many previously unknown genetic interactions and providing insight into gene function and drug–target relationships that could enable the development of new therapies for tuberculosis.

title: Conjugation-regulated self-assembled molecules for tandem solar cells
abstract:
Rationally engineered molecular spatial conjugation is used for the formation of highly ordered, conformal self-assembled molecules, enabling the fabrication of high-performance perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells. 
 Perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells on rough textured substrates are at present limited by a critical trade-off in self-assembled monolayer (SAM) design because increasing molecular conjugation enhances conductivity but often leads to unfavourable aggregation that impairs conformal coverage1,2. Here we overcome this challenge using a rationally engineered molecular spatial conjugation that incorporates tailored intramolecular distortion to suppress excess π–π stacking without sacrificing charge-transport efficiency. This steric regulation facilitates the formation of a highly ordered, conformal SAM across rough pyramidal textures. By reconciling molecular packing with interfacial coverage, the tailored interface provides optimized energy-level alignment for ultrafast charge extraction, enables improved defect passivation through adaptive conformational adjustment and acts as a robust template for high-quality perovskite film growth. Making use of this interface, the optimized tandem device achieves a notable fill factor (FF) of 85%, yielding a certified stabilized power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 35.1%. Furthermore, the device demonstrates outstanding stability, retaining more than 94% of its initial performance after 1,500 h of ageing under the ISOS-L-1 protocol. Our findings provide a clear molecular engineering route to reconcile conductivity and film uniformity while maximizing the performance of tandem photovoltaics on textured silicon substrates. Rationally engineered molecular spatial conjugation is used for the formation of highly ordered, conformal self-assembled molecules, enabling the fabrication of high-performance perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells.

title: Hard X-ray attosecond metrology
abstract:
Metrology techniques are developed to characterize and control attosecond hard X-ray pulses, directly measuring a 170-attosecond duration and enabling ultrafast studies of electronic dynamics in quantum systems. 
 Sub-ångström spatial resolution combined with attosecond temporal resolution enables direct observation of electron motion in matter1. Attosecond hard X-ray pulses generated at X-ray free-electron laser sources provide the requisite spatiotemporal sensitivity, yet their application has been limited by the absence of precise pulse metrology and control. Here, building on a broadband X-ray split-delay line, we establish metrology of attosecond hard X-ray pulses. Field-correlation measurements provide the first time-domain characterization of the pulse coherence time and demonstrate attosecond synchronization between the generated pulse pairs. By exploiting non-sequential two-photon absorption as a nonlinear probe, intensity autocorrelation quantifies the average pulse duration directly in the time domain to be 170 as. The demonstrated experimental tools and techniques enable systematic attosecond time-resolved experiments, including X-ray pump–X-ray probe spectroscopy and diffraction, and open a pathway to probing electronic phenomena with unprecedented spatial-temporal resolution. Metrology techniques are developed to characterize and control attosecond hard X-ray pulses, directly measuring a 170-attosecond duration and enabling ultrafast studies of electronic dynamics in quantum systems.

title: Cancer-selective gene circuits via intrinsic ribosomal frameshifting
abstract:
Codon-pair-dependent ribosomal frameshifting is a feature of translational dysregulation in cancer cells. 
 Ribosomal frameshifting, an uncommon translational recoding event, is best known for its regulatory roles in viral gene expression1,2, whereas its physiological relevance in mammals remains poorly understood. Here we show that specific codon pairs trigger efficient −1 frameshifting preferentially in cancer cells. Mechanistically, this recoding arises from ribosomal pausing associated with tRNA and amino acid availability, and is amplified by impaired ribosome quality control and sustained phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6. We found that this codon-pair-specific frameshifting represents an intrinsic state of translational dysregulation, which is prevalent across cancer cells and reshapes protein synthesis. Taking advantage of this frameshifting-permissive state in cancer cells, we engineered a frameshifting-activated synthetic therapeutic circuit (FAST) that conditionally expresses the pyroptotic effector gasdermin D. FAST is activated across diverse cancer cell types, inducing potent and selective pyroptosis, while sparing normal tissues from detectable toxicity. As a proof of concept, systemic AAV9-mediated delivery of FAST in mouse models of colorectal and pancreatic cancer elicited pronounced tumour regression, robust immune activation and synergistic effects with immune checkpoint blockade. Collectively, these findings reveal codon-pair-dependent ribosomal frameshifting as a feature of translational dysregulation in cancer cells and establish translation-coupled gene circuits as a strategy for cancer-selective therapy. title: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
abstract:
Genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals are analysed, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which alternative archaeological and linguistic models for the origin and spread of Celtic fit reconstructed demographic histories. 
 Celtic languages are today restricted to Europe’s Atlantic fringes but were widely spoken across the continent during the Iron Age1–3. How Celtic achieved this early distribution remains contested4, with alternative archaeological and linguistic models proposing different homelands and dispersal routes. Here we analyse genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which these models fit reconstructed demographic histories. We identify three main processes shaping European population structure that are relevant to the Celtic dispersal. First, the arrival of Steppe-related ancestry with Bell Beaker-associated groups after around 4400 bp (calibrated years before present or 1950 ce) across the region in which Celtic and related languages were later spoken. Second, a movement from southwestern Europe into Britain during the Bronze Age (3800–3200 bp), consistent with scenarios in which Celtic formed along the Atlantic façade. Third, a westward expansion of ancestry related to Late Bronze Age Knovíz–Urnfield-associated populations from eastern central Europe (3200–2800 bp), affecting France, the British Isles, northeastern Iberia and Italy and later associated with Iron Age Hallstatt and La Tène contexts5–8. Although all three movements have parallels with proposed models, we argue that the final movement, from eastern central Europe, is most parsimonious for the spread of Celtic. Although human history does not necessarily follow a parsimonious trajectory9 and language shifts need not track genetic change, these results delimit the demographic scenarios that are plausible for the emergence of Celtic in prehistoric Europe. title: Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling
abstract:
Longitudinal tracking of endothelial cells shows they can adapt to loss of VEGFR2 and form new functional vessels, challenging conventional views of the essential role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and providing insight into resistance to anti-VEGF therapies. 
 The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) ligand and its main receptor VEGFR2 are considered to be essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, sprouting and survival1. Blood vessels cannot form in growing embryos or tissues when VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is compromised in all cells2,3. The anti-VEGF antibody, which can block angiogenesis in cancer, wound healing or ischaemic diseases, is among the most widely used antibodies in the clinic. However, vascular resistance to anti-VEGF therapy has been reported4,5. Here we used iFlpMosaics and iSuRe–HadCre to induce and track genetic mosaics of endothelial cells (ECs) lacking VEGFR2 during the entire embryonic and postnatal development. These Vegfr2-knockout (Vegfr2KO) ECs adapted, proliferated normally and competed with wild-type cells over time, eventually forming a substantial portion of the vascular network in most organs. Vegfr2KO ECs could not sprout during the first wave of angiogenesis in most tissues, because this process is highly VEGF-dependent and favours growth and mobilization of wild-type ECs. However, owing to their inability to respond to VEGF, Vegfr2KO ECs became dominant in veins, which represented a long-term and continuous source of ECs for subsequent waves of VEGF-independent angiogenesis. Comparative single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of ECs with acute and long-term loss of VEGFR2 identified both common and organ-specific molecular mechanisms of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss. These included significant endothelial venousization and upregulation of ligands for VEGFR1 and VEGFR3. VEGFR1 only partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss in capillary ECs, whereas VEGFR3 compensated only in arterial ECs. Loss of the three VEGF receptors did not compromise venous growth. Notably, loss of the master regulator of venous development, NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), significantly compromised expansion of Vegfr2KO ECs. This work has implications for our understanding of the role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and demonstrates venousization as a mechanism of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss during angiogenesis. Longitudinal tracking of endothelial cells shows they can adapt to loss of VEGFR2 and form new functional vessels, challenging conventional views of the essential role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and providing insight into resistance to anti-VEGF therapies.

title: The neural basis of flavour–nutrient learning
abstract:
A dopamine pathway to the basolateral amygdala is necessary for associating nutrients with flavours. 
 Animals learn about the external world in part through interoceptive signals1,2. For example, the nutrient content of food is first estimated in the mouth, in the form of flavour, and then it is measured again through slower signals from the gut. How these signals from the mouth and gut are integrated to drive learning is unclear. Here we identify a dopamine (DA) pathway that enables learning about the nutrient content of food. We show that DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area are necessary for associating nutrients with flavours, and that post-ingestive nutrients trigger DA release selectively in a small region of the anterior basolateral amygdala (BLA) but not in canonical DA targets in striatum. This nutrient-triggered DA release occurs preferentially in the left BLA in mice, and this same structure is preferentially activated by post-ingestive nutrients in humans. We identify the gut sensors that are responsible for nutrient-triggered DA release; show that they activate BLA-projecting DA neurons defined by expression of cholecystokinin; and demonstrate that stimulation of DA axon terminals in the anterior BLA drives flavour–nutrient learning but not other aspects of feeding behaviour. Two-photon imaging of neurons in the left anterior BLA reveals that they integrate gustatory and post-ingestive cues, and silencing these neurons prevents flavour–nutrient learning. These findings establish a neural basis for how animals learn about the nutrient content of their food. A dopamine pathway to the basolateral amygdala is necessary for associating nutrients with flavours.

title: Nectin-4 mediates rubella virus entry in airway and placental cells
abstract:
Nectin-4 is identified as a pivotal host entry receptor for respiratory transmission and early placental infection of rubella virus. 
 Rubella virus (RuV) causes rubella and, when acquired during pregnancy, congenital rubella syndrome1. Despite its clinical significance, the cellular entry mechanism of RuV remains poorly characterized, owing to limited identification of host receptors2, which hinders pathogenesis research and therapeutic development. Here, using proximity biotin labelling-based proteomics coupled with CRISPR–Cas9 validation, we identify nectin-4 as a functional RuV entry receptor. Ectopic expression of nectin-4 conferred susceptibility to RuV in non-permissive cells, whereas blocking or genetic ablation of nectin-4 reduced infection, results that demonstrate that nectin-4 is a major entry factor. Mechanistically, nectin-4 directly interacts with the RuV envelope glycoprotein heterodimer and facilitates receptor-mediated endocytosis following initial calcium-dependent viral attachment to cellular lipids. In polarized airway epithelial models, nectin-4 mediates basolateral entry of RuV and supports apical progeny release, a finding that provides a molecular mechanism for respiratory transmission. In placental models, nectin-4 is highly expressed on syncytiotrophoblasts and facilitates infection at the maternal–fetal interface, although additional nectin-4-independent pathways contribute to infection of other trophoblast populations. Together, these data establish nectin-4 as a key factor for respiratory transmission and early placental infection of RuV and highlight it as a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of rubella and related diseases. Nectin-4 is identified as a pivotal host entry receptor for respiratory transmission and early placental infection of rubella virus.

title: Aggression experience and observation drive shared behavioural and neural changes
abstract:
Aggression experience and observation recruit a brain-wide network of excitatory, inhibitory and valence signals, and changes to this activation pattern predict a shared adaptive behaviour-control policy in a new aggression context. 
 The ability to observe the social behaviour of others and use observed information to bias future action is a fundamental building block of social cognition1–3. Aggression observation activates hypothalamic neurons relevant for aggression control4,5, but whether observation and experience engage common circuit mechanisms that promote a new shared behavioural policy is unclear. Here we develop a strategy to perform large-scale cell-type-specific recordings across subcortical networks for social behaviour generation and learning. We record longitudinally while animals train through direct aggression experience or observation, then probe shared differences in behaviour and neural activity in a novel aggression context. After training, we detect unique signatures of a shared adaptive behavioural strategy that is absent in animals without training. During aggression observation, observed behaviour recruits widespread activation across subcortical networks for behavioural generation and mimics activity evoked by experienced behaviour, and shared neural changes persist into the novel aggression context. Multiregion modelling reveals shared changes to a core aggression network across both experience and observation, including a widespread reduction in inhibition, which we find is necessary for adaptive behavioural change. Together, this demonstrates that experience-like activity during aggression observation can recruit a shared inhibitory plasticity mechanism that biases behaviour toward adaptive proactive behavioural strategies. Aggression experience and observation recruit a brain-wide network of excitatory, inhibitory and valence signals, and changes to this activation pattern predict a shared adaptive behaviour-control policy in a new aggression context.

title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism
abstract:
Gene network analysis shows how mutations in diverse genes associated with autism spectrum disorder can converge to exert shared effects, with X-linked transcription factor ZFX emerging as a key protective factor in the female brain. 
 Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD1–3. Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge4. Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in male than in female individuals5, and female autistic people tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared with their male counterparts6,7; however, the biological basis of this ‘female protective effect’ (FPE) has remained unknown8,9. Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network enabled identification of central transcriptional regulators that drive this transcriptomic convergence, including prominent ASD gene CHD8 and candidates including REST. Furthermore, X-linked transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in female individuals10, emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in the female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the female protective effect. Together, these results show how key gene regulatory networks can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD. title: The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity
abstract:
Continental-scale uplift and subsidence associated with long-wavelength dynamic topography due to mantle convection drove the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity. 
 The Great Unconformity marks a globally extensive erosive surface linked to climatic shifts1 and environmental transitions2 that preceded the Cambrian explosion of life. The processes proposed to explain the formation of the Great Unconformity include glacial erosion during the Snowball Earth1,3,4, rifting and plume activity5–7, sea-level fall8 and mantle-driven dynamic topography6,9–11. However, the dynamics of these processes have not been tested. Here we show that continental-scale uplift and subsidence associated with long-wavelength dynamic topography12 due to mantle convection drove the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity. Our models predict prolonged continental-scale Neoproterozoic uplift and long-term Phanerozoic subsidence for Laurentia, Baltica and North China. This vertical motion scenario is ideal for the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity, which is a first-order surface expression of deep Earth processes. The predicted prolonged continental uplift throughout Cryogenian times would have resulted in marked erosion due to the action of glaciers13. The large area of Laurentia and limited deformation at its margins explain why the Great Unconformity is best preserved and documented there. Our models predict cycles of dynamic topography that are broadly reflected in preserved sediment volume across continents1,14, and open new avenues for understanding the environments of Cambrian animal diversification. Continental-scale uplift and subsidence associated with long-wavelength dynamic topography due to mantle convection drove the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity.

title: Twist-angle-dependent quantum phase diagrams in moiré bilayer MoTe<sub>2</sub>
abstract:
Twist-angle-dependent studies of moiré bilayer MoTe2 reveal a transition from fractional topological states to correlated insulators and superconductivity, linking topology, symmetry breaking and magnetism in moiré quantum materials. 
 Two-dimensional semiconducting moiré superlattices provide a highly tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated and topological quantum phases1–5. As a prototypical example, twisted bilayer MoTe2 (tMoTe2) has been shown to host fractional topological phases at zero magnetic field6–20. However, their evolution with twist angle and competition with other correlated quantum states remain largely unexplored. Here we report a systematic transport study of twist-angle-dependent phase diagrams in tMoTe2 across a range of 3.79°–5.76°, revealing an evolution from valley-polarized, fractional topological states to valley-degenerate correlated states and superconductivity. At relatively small twist angles, partially filled Chern bands of tMoTe2 host fractional quantum anomalous Hall states following the Jain sequence, together with signatures of an anomalous composite Fermi liquid at moiré hole filling factor νh = 1/2. Increasing twist angle progressively suppresses fractional topological phases and reconstructs the half-filled Chern band into symmetry-breaking integer Chern insulating states. At νh = 1, we observe a transition from robust integer quantum anomalous Hall insulators at small angles to displacement-field-tuned, topologically trivial correlated insulators at larger angles. At twist angles above approximately 5.6°, superconductivity emerges adjacent to the νh = 1 correlated insulator, with a phase diagram closely resembling that recently reported in twisted bilayer WSe2 (refs. 21–24). Our results indicate a unified twist-angle-driven phase evolution linking fractional topology, symmetry breaking, magnetic order and superconductivity, providing new insight into the emergent quantum phenomena in moiré systems. title: An open structure-guided RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction
abstract:
structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model pre-trained on 21 million sequence–structure pairs, learns multimodal representations that improve secondary and tertiary structure prediction, functional inference and zero-shot generalization across diverse RNA families. 
 RNA language models have achieved strong performance across diverse downstream tasks by leveraging large-scale sequence data. However, RNA function is fundamentally shaped by hierarchical structure, making structural information important for pre-training. Existing approaches often depend on noisy annotations or task-specific objectives that can limit generalizability. Here we present structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model trained on 21 million RNA sequence–structure pairs by integrating base-pairing interactions into masked language modelling through a pair-matching operation. We also introduce MUSES, a multi-source ensemble of secondary structures designed to mitigate predictor bias, and a dynamic masking ratio that balances structure-guided and nucleotide-level masking. structRFM learns joint sequence and structure representations as sequence-level, nucleotide-level and pairwise features for broad downstream adaptation. It ranks highly in zero-shot homology classification and establishes new benchmarks for secondary-structure prediction. Its tertiary-structure adaptation, Zfold, consistently improves both three-dimensional predictions and their extracted secondary structures, with performance comparable to AlphaFold31 across CASP15-natural, CASP16 and RNA-Puzzles. structRFM also improves performance on function-prediction tasks and generalizes to newly released RNA families and long non-coding RNAs. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of structure-guided pre-training and highlight multimodal RNA language models for robust structural and functional inference. The complete 21-million-pair dataset, model weights and source code are openly available to support multimodal RNA foundation-model development. structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model pre-trained on 21 million sequence–structure pairs, learns multimodal representations that improve secondary and tertiary structure prediction, functional inference and zero-shot generalization across diverse RNA families.

title: Synergy in viral–bacterial co-infection expedites algal bloom demise
abstract:
Viral–bacterial synergy accelerates algal bloom collapse by enhancing virus-induced mortality, driven by Alteromonas chemoattraction and co-infection, revealing a previously unrecognized mortality agent that influences oceanic carbon cycling . 
 Algal bloom demise, often caused by viruses, is a major driver of carbon cycling in the surface ocean1,2. However, although blooms collapse synchronously, fewer than 30% of algal cells are actively infected by viruses3, indicating the involvement of additional mortality agents. Here we quantified tripartite interactions within a synthetic community composed of the abundant coccolithophore Gephyrocapsa huxleyi, bacteria and viruses isolated during a bloom. We found that bacteria significantly enhanced virus-induced algal mortality in G. huxleyi as well as in three other globally widespread microalgae. We quantified this interaction using two new metrics: the synergy index, which measures viral–bacterial interaction strength, and the benefit index, which assesses changes in bacterial fitness. We identified Alteromonas bacteria as drivers of viral–bacterial co-infection, with consistently high synergy index and benefit index. We found that during algal blooms, Alteromonas displayed high chemoattraction towards infected cell extracts, accumulated in aggregates derived from bloom demise, and increased in abundance during oceanic bloom collapse. Viral–bacterial synergy represents a previously unrecognized mortality agent that controls bloom termination, modulating the balance between the carbon-recycling viral shunt and the carbon-exporting viral shuttle pathways, which influence global carbon cycling4–6. title: A conserved flowering-time module underlies double-season cropping
abstract:
The genomic footprints of 80 years of modern breeding in China are traced using representative cultivars, demonstrating how precision genome editing can be used to reconstruct adaptive modules for climate-resilient crop design. 
 Adapting crops to intensive cultivation systems under climate change requires varieties that combine yield potential with optimized flowering and maturation1,2. In central and eastern China, barley has long been cultivated in a double-season cropping system, in which early flowering and maturation are critical for escaping presummer terminal heat stress and enabling flexible rotation with summer crops3,4. Here we trace the genomic footprints of 80 years of modern breeding in China using 505 representative cultivars and identify a flowering-time module defined by a single amino acid substitution in PHYTOCHROME C in combination with a winter-type VERNALIZATION 1 haplotype that underpins this adaptation. The derived allele accelerates heading and maturity, and its frequency has risen sharply in modern autumn-sown varieties. Using base editing in barley and wheat, we confirm causality and demonstrate that this flowering-time combination module, PhyC–VRN1, is functionally conserved across Triticeae. Our results identify and experimentally validate a breeding-relevant flowering-time module that has been selected during modern breeding to enable intensive crop rotations, as well as demonstrate how precision genome editing can be used to reconstruct such adaptive modules for climate-resilient crop design. title: Microbiome-wide PheWAS links gut microbial SNVs to health and exposures
abstract:
Gut microbial single-nucleotide variants across 10,781 individuals reveal 940 associations that link strain-level genetic variation to 69 host traits, with structural analyses pinpointing host phenotype-associated variants, providing a base pair-resolution resource for mechanistic hypothesis generation. 
 Alterations in the microbial composition of the human gut have been associated with a wide range of chronic diseases1,2. Yet species-level composition alone can obscure extensive within-species genetic diversity and functional variation. This has driven a shift towards strain-resolved, genetic-level analysis of the microbiome, leveraging microbial genetic variation to identify disease-relevant genes and pathways3–6. Here we conducted a phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) analysing 12.8 million gut microbial single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) with 244 host health phenotypes and environmental exposures in 10,781 individuals from 6 independent cohorts. We identify 940 independent associations across 69 host factors, including age, sex and cardiovascular and metabolic parameters. Structural analyses identified host-phenotype-associated SNVs in functionally important regions of proteins, findings that inform mechanistic hypotheses about how microbial genetic changes relate to environmental and host physiological factors. For example, we identified an age-associated SNV in Faecalibacterium prausnitzii that affects an amino acid within the protein pocket that binds glutathione. To support future efforts, all study summary statistics are provided in an online catalogue (
              https://fulab.web.rug.nl/SNV-MWAS/
              
            ). Together, these results identify new biological connections between the human host and microbial genetic variants at base pair resolution and provide a resource for hypothesis generation that will aid future understanding of the strain-level functionality of the gut microbiota. title: A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity
abstract:
A deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma is generated, pairing transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling, and tracing glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity to a stereotyped and spatially patterned trajectory of cancer cells. 
 Cancer cells show highly heterogeneous and plastic states in glioblastoma, an incurable brain tumour1–5. However, how these malignant states arise and whether they follow defined cellular trajectories across tumours is poorly understood. Here we generated a deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma that pairs transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling of 12 tumours across many regions. We identify that glioblastoma heterogeneity is driven by spatially patterned transitions of cancer cells from developmental-like states towards those defined by a glial injury response and hypoxia. This cellular trajectory regionalizes tumours into distinct tissue microenvironments and manifests in a molecularly conserved manner across tumours as well as genetically distinct tumour subclones. Consistently, using a new deep-learning framework to map cancer cell states jointly with clones in situ, we show that tumour subclones are finely spatially intermixed through glioblastoma tissue microenvironments. We validate this cellular trajectory by using somatic mutation-based hierarchies in vivo and an experimental patient-derived organoid model ex vivo. Finally, we show that this cancer cell trajectory is intimately linked to myeloid heterogeneity and unfolds across regionalized myeloid signalling environments. Our findings define a stereotyped trajectory of cancer cells in glioblastoma and unify glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity into a tractable cellular and tissue framework. A deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma is generated, pairing transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling, and tracing glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity to a stereotyped and spatially patterned trajectory of cancer cells.

title: Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit
abstract:
A new physics-based method combining the use of automatic differentiation to optimize millions of model parameters with a flexible physical model is described for starlight subtraction from real, on-sky coronagraphic images to greatly improve sensitivity. 
 Exoplanet imaging is the main method for detailed characterization of planets orbiting beyond 1 au (ref. 1) but it requires suppressing the bright glare of the star to see the faint planet light. As well as sophisticated instrumentation2,3, effective image processing is necessary for starlight suppression, which continues to be a substantial limitation4. Standard algorithms use reference images for starlight modelling and thus they are limited by inevitable telescope instabilities that change from reference to science observation5,6. Addressing this challenge will increase the number of planets amenable to direct imaging and will be a notable step towards imaging exo-Earths with future observatories7. Here we present a new physics-based method for starlight subtraction. Our method combines a multistep optimization with a flexible physical model to produce a starlight model, allowing modelling and compensation of instrument instabilities. We use automatic differentiation (autodiff)8 to optimize millions of model parameters. We demonstrate our method on observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) Near-InfraRed Camera (NIRCam)9–11 coronagraph instrument. We achieve sensitivity 2–15 times superior to standard techniques, including the first detection of 51 Eridani b (ref. 12) at 4.3 μm. This is the first time, to our knowledge, that such an approach has demonstrated substantially improved sensitivity on real, on-sky coronagraphic imaging. Our framework can be extended to other current and future ground-based and space-based observatories, including the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), potentially relaxing the unprecedented stability requirements needed to make these a success. title: Seismic evidence for double slab tears at the Neo-Tethyan subduction–collision transition
abstract:
The slab at the transition between the Makran subduction and Zagros collision zones in southeastern Iran is torn in two places, which may accommodate the differential plate motion, according to an interpretation of seismic tomographic imaging. 
 The transition from oceanic subduction to continental collision is a key stage in the Wilson Cycle. Yet, key processes governing this transition remain unclear owing to sparse observations of structure at depth. One such process is detachment of the subducting slab, which influences both deformation and magmatism in the overriding plate. Here we present seismic tomographic images that we interpret as evidence for two slab tears beneath southeastern Iran, where the Neo-Tethys Ocean is closing. Specifically, we show that in the Makran subduction zone, the oceanic lithosphere has continuously subducted to depths of at least 450 km, whereas in the Zagros collision zone to the west, the continental lithosphere has subducted no deeper than 300 km, resulting in east–southward slab tearing and detachment. We further identify another slab tear that probably initiated at the junction between the Makran Trench and the transform boundary and has propagated southward as the continental plate advances northward. The coexistence of these two tearing modes provides a rare snapshot of the short-lived early transition from oceanic subduction to continental collision. The slab at the transition between the Makran subduction and Zagros collision zones in southeastern Iran is torn in two places, which may accommodate the differential plate motion, according to an interpretation of seismic tomographic imaging.

title: Entangled-to-packed crossover in nonlinear extensional rheology of entangled polymers
abstract:
Entanglements among long-chain macromolecules dictate the mechanical performance of polymeric materials and are described with the tube model but the validity of this model has been questioned for nonlinear extension. Here the authors reveal the key mechanism that governs the mechanical response during extension by elucidating the evolution of entanglements using computer simulations and theoretical analysis. 
 The tube model, which reduces the interaction of many-chain entanglement to a single-chain picture, has enabled quantitative descriptions of the mechanical behaviors of polymeric materials and underpins applications from polymer processing to life sciences. In strong extensional flows, however, this theory systematically fails. Herein, through molecular dynamics simulations of entangled polymers, we reveal a strain-induced crossover from the entangled state to a packed state in the inter-chain configuration. Following the saturation of primitive chain stretch, convective disentanglement and chain alignment reorganize the system into a packed configuration of aligned segments. This crossover makes an explicit inter-chain contribution necessary for describing tensile stress beyond the intra-chain conformational stress, explaining the breakdown of tube-based descriptions and quantitatively capturing the mechanical response at large extensional strains. These findings clearly show how the inter-chain reorganization governs the nonlinear extensional behaviors. Entanglements among long-chain macromolecules dictate the mechanical performance of polymeric materials and are described with the tube model but the validity of this model has been questioned for nonlinear extension. Here the authors reveal the key mechanism that governs the mechanical response during extension by elucidating the evolution of entanglements using computer simulations and theoretical analysis.

title: Diacylglycerol Metabolism Drives Host–pathogen Responses During Enteric Infection in Drosophila
abstract:
Li et al. reveal a lipid-dependent signaling axis that links intestinal epithelial cells and intestinal muscle to gut motility and bacterial pathogen clearance, offering mechanistic insight into how lipid dynamics orchestrate host defenses. 
 Lipid metabolism is fundamental to cellular homeostasis, supporting energy storage, membrane architecture, and cellular signaling. Beyond these canonical roles, lipids have emerged as critical regulators of host immunity. Here, we define a lipid-driven mechanism that governs host–pathogen interactions by impacting pathogen clearance and thus infection outcomes. Exploiting Drosophila, we show that enteric infection triggers robust accumulation of neutral lipids, and specifically 1,2-diacylglycerols (DAGs), in the midgut. Disruption of DAG biosynthesis or lipid transport in midgut enterocytes (ECs) impairs lipid accumulation and reduces host survival. Conversely, dietary lipid supplementation enhances lipid storage and improves survival. Mechanistically, these lipid-dependent responses regulate defecation, thereby controlling bacterial clearance from the midgut. DAGs can act as signaling lipids that activate protein kinase C (PKC), and DAG accumulation in ECs correlates with elevated PKC activity and calcium signaling in midgut visceral muscle (VM), promoting VM contraction, midgut motility, and expulsion of pathogens via defecation. Together, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for DAG metabolism in shaping host defenses. Li et al. reveal a lipid-dependent signaling axis that links intestinal epithelial cells and intestinal muscle to gut motility and bacterial pathogen clearance, offering mechanistic insight into how lipid dynamics orchestrate host defenses.

title: Engineering filamentous myosins for optical control of contractility
abstract:
Zemsky and colleagues employ protein engineering to create filamentous myosins controlled by light. These optogenetic motors enable spatiotemporal control of contractility in vitro and in cells, providing a tool for probing contractile actomyosin systems. 
 Understanding the behaviors of contractile actomyosin systems requires precise spatiotemporal control of filamentous myosin activity. Here, we develop a tool for optical control of contractility by extending the MyLOV family of gearshifting motors to create engineered filamentous myosins that change velocity in response to blue light. We characterize these minifilaments using in vitro single-molecule tracking assays, contractility assays in reconstituted actin networks, and imaging of contractile phenotypes in live cells. In vitro, gearshifting minifilaments change speed and/or direction when illuminated, and contraction rates of minifilaments in actin networks can be modulated using blue light. In cells, gearshifting minifilaments enable optical control of protrusion retraction, cortical flow, and cell migration. Finally, we develop an alternative design for minifilaments that only interact processively with actin in blue light. Engineered minifilaments could be used to dissect behaviors such as self-organization and mechanotransduction in contractile systems both in vitro and in cells and tissues. title: Energy-guided combinatorial co-optimization of antibody affinity and stability
abstract:
Here, Tennenhouse et al. develop LAffAb, a structure-based method for designing CDR mutations to improve affinity and developability. By filtering mutations predicted to disrupt stability and foldability, LAffAb enables accurate, one-shot design. 
 Affinity maturation is an essential process in antibody engineering. Although powerful, it is iterative, time-consuming, and can result in trade-offs, where affinity is gained at the cost of important properties, such as specificity and stability. We present a scalable strategy, called LAffAb, that starts from a crystallographic structure of the antibody-antigen complex and introduces combinations of mutations to the antibody to optimize the energy of the complex. A combinatorial library comprising 7000 variants with up to nine mutations results in gains of up to 30-fold in affinity while co-optimizing stability. Surprisingly, the library does not converge on a single solution, instead favoring diverse variants with a high mutational load. Small-scale screening of 10 designs against a potential drug target improves affinity by an order-of-magnitude while maintaining high developability. We also apply LAffAb to improve the developability of a therapeutic antibody while maintaining affinity. We envision that LAffAb can be used to design stable, specific, and high-affinity binders and to improve our understanding of sequence, structure, and function relationships in antibodies. Here, Tennenhouse et al. develop LAffAb, a structure-based method for designing CDR mutations to improve affinity and developability. By filtering mutations predicted to disrupt stability and foldability, LAffAb enables accurate, one-shot design.

title: Multiscale neural dynamics reveal how striatal subregions shape stress vulnerability and resilience
abstract:
This study shows that striatal subregions shape individual differences in stress vulnerability and resilience through distinct patterns of multiscale network dynamics during stress coping. 
 Effective stress coping relies on neural and endocrine coordination, with the mesostriatal system serving as a central substrate. However, how striatal subregions contribute to stress vulnerability versus resilience remains unclear. Here, we show dissociable roles of the nucleus accumbens (NAC) and dorsal caudate (dCA) and their associated brain networks in shaping stress responses. We identify neural stability (NS)—capturing stress-induced changes in state-switching frequency over the course of stress responses—as a marker: task-state NS correlates positively with stress-related NAC activity, whereas resting-state NS correlates inversely with stress-related dCA activity. NAC-mediated networks and associated NS further predict faster cortisol recovery. Intriguingly, NAC-related functional connectivity patterns spatially covary with dopamine D2 receptor distributions and gene expression in inhibitory neurons and glia, whereas dCA-related patterns covary with μ-opioid receptor distributions. Together, these findings reveal striatal subregional heterogeneity in stress coping and characterize resilience as a multisystem homeostatic process integrating neural, endocrine, and molecular layers. This study shows that striatal subregions shape individual differences in stress vulnerability and resilience through distinct patterns of multiscale network dynamics during stress coping.

title: Strong-gain water-window X-ray laser driven by plasma photocathode wakefield acceleration
abstract:
Plasma wakefield accelerators promise compact X-ray lasers but have so far lacked sufficiently bright, stable electron beams. The authors show that beam loading by plasma photocathode-injected electron beams boosts brightness and self-stabilises acceleration inside wakefields, paving the way to compact, robust water-window X-ray lasers. 
 X-ray free-electron lasers are large and complex machines, limited by electron beam brightness. Here we show through start-to-end simulations how to realise compact, robust and tunable X-ray lasers in the water window, based on ultra-bright electron beams from plasma wakefield accelerators. First, an ultra-low-emittance electron beam is released by a plasma photocathode in a metre-scale plasma wakefield accelerator. By tuning the beam charge, space-charge forces create a balance between beam fields and wakefields that reduces beam energy spread and improves energy stability – both critical for beam extraction, transport, and focusing into a metre-scale undulator. Here, the resulting ultra-bright beams produce wavelength-tunable, coherent, femtosecond-scale photon pulses at strong gain. This regime enables reliable generation of multi-gigawatt-class X-ray laser pulses across the water window, offering tunability via the witness beam charge and robustness against variations in plasma wakefield strength and plasma photocathode laser jitter. Our findings help democratise access to coherent, high-power, soft X-ray radiation. Plasma wakefield accelerators promise compact X-ray lasers but have so far lacked sufficiently bright, stable electron beams. The authors show that beam loading by plasma photocathode-injected electron beams boosts brightness and self-stabilises acceleration inside wakefields, paving the way to compact, robust water-window X-ray lasers.

title: Global Rossby wave rivers connecting remote wave activity to the East Asian summer monsoon
abstract:
Global Rossby wave rivers connecting remote wave activity to the East Asian summer monsoon 
 We introduce a sink-oriented Rossby wave river (WR) framework that traces remote wave activity along continuous propagation pathways converging toward specific sinks, and use the Li-Yang wave ray flux to diagnose the global WRs converging into the East Asian summer monsoon (EASM) region. At 850 hPa, Southern Hemisphere and pan-tropical pathways dominate and converge near the Philippines; at 500 hPa, low-latitude easterly and midlatitude westerly WRs become comparable in strength; at 200 hPa, WR propagation becomes concentrated along the jet waveguide. Strikingly, the two major 500-hPa WRs undergo nearly head-on confluence, forming a climatological Rossby wave front that closely coincides with the Meiyu front. Vertically, the dominant pathway shifts from the southern monsoon channel below to the northwestern westerly waveguide aloft, with the transition occurring above the Meiyu–Changma–Baiu rainband. This sink-oriented perspective reframes EASM teleconnections as an interconnected global wave-propagation network linking remote Rossby wave sources to regional climate impacts.

title: Responses of surface radiative balance to wildfires differ across ecosystems
abstract:
Responses of surface radiative balance to wildfires differ across ecosystems 
 Wildfires alter land surface albedo and temperature, modulating the radiative budget and climate. Previous studies have predominantly reported enhanced shortwave absorption induced by post-fire surface darkening over forests. Here, using two-decade (2001–2020) satellite observations of wildfires, we show that post-fire summer surface albedo and radiative balance shifts vary significantly across ecosystems. Broadleaf forests and grasslands exhibit a brightening effect, because the exposure of bright soils and rapid vegetation regrowth outweigh the deposition of dark carbonaceous residues. The post-fire surface brightening then amplifies the warming-driven radiative cooling. Conversely, in needleleaf forests, shrublands, and savannas, post-fire surface darkening increases shortwave absorption, yet warming-driven longwave radiative losses remain dominant, leading to net radiative cooling. Surface radiative fluxes exhibit high sensitivity to fire size in mid-to-high latitude regions driven by distinct fire-ecosystem feedbacks. Therefore, the ecosystem heterogeneity must be considered when assessing the effects of wildfires on the surface radiative budget and climate.

title: Loss of snow persistence during late season drives snow-season shortening in Northeast China under global warming
abstract:
The loss of snow persistence during late winter to spring across Northeast China leads to shorter snow season under global warming, as suggested by bias-corrected CMIP6 climate projections based on Satellite-constrained machine learning framework. 
 Northeast China lies on a mid-latitude boundary where small warming can shift snowfall to rain and shorten the snow season, but climate models often simulate snow fields with large regional biases. Here we show that satellite-constrained, 1-km machine-learning emulators project snow-cover duration without directly using modeled snow variables. They relate observed daily snow cover during 2001–2020 to temperature, precipitation, snowfall fraction and terrain, and are driven by bias-corrected climate projections. Snow seasons shorten almost everywhere, with more than 98% of land grid cells agreeing on the sign of change. By 2081–2100, domain-mean snow-cover duration decreases by 42, 64, and 85 days under low-, intermediate- and high-emission pathways, respectively, and areas with fewer than 50 snow days expand from 19% to 99% under high emissions. Snow-season shortening is dominated by loss of late-winter and spring snow persistence, especially at low–middle elevations and along the present rain–snow transition zone. title: High flow capacity and low viscosity of the Séítah formation, at Jezero Crater, Mars
abstract:
Olivine cumulate lava flows within Jerezo Crater behaved as low viscosity flows due to the reduced gravity of Mars compared to Earth, according to dynamic flow modelling and petrographic data from the Perseverance rover 
 The discovery of olivine cumulate at the Séítah Formation within Jezero Crater was one of the most unexpected findings of the Mars2020 Perseverance rover mission thus far. We use rover geochemistry data to calculate the viscosity and relative flow distance of the Séítah unit and its parental lava. Compared to Earth, Mars has lower gravity, current atmosphere and crustal volatile content. These factors imply commensurate changes in lava flow dynamics that need to be better understood. We suggest the Séítah olivine cumulate discovered by the rover was related to a ponded lava flow, based on the low viscosity and distribution of the unit. We estimate an approximate relative depth for the cumulate layer of the lava pond using a convective lava magma model. We also compare the Noachian Jezero olivine rich viscosities to Hesperian basalts analysed by Spirit, and find the Noachian samples to have a greater propensity to flow than their younger cousins. Future observations of the olivine rich unit and laboratory studies of the samples collected by Mars2020 will provide a key window into the flow dynamics and evolution of Martian lava flows. title: Sustained crustal helium enrichment associated with postseismic viscoelastic relaxation following the 2025 Myanmar earthquake
abstract:
Slip during the 2025 M7.7 Myanmar earthquake triggered high He-emissions that may persist for several decades along the Red River Fault, located around 600 km away from the epicentre, according to elevated gas-phase He concentrations in thermal-spring groundwater. 
 Earthquakes can alter fluid flow far from a rupture, but the processes that sustain such changes for months remain uncertain. Here we report a sustained increase in gas-phase helium concentration at a thermal spring on the Red River Fault, about 600 kilometres from the 2025 magnitude 7.7 Myanmar earthquake. Minute-scale monitoring recorded intermittent fluctuations before the earthquake and a progressive concentration increase afterwards. Groundwater level, rainfall, atmospheric pressure and conservative estimates of instrumental drift do not reproduce this evolution. He–Ne isotope measurements from a nearby spring indicate that the added helium was predominantly radiogenic and crustal, with no resolvable increase in mantle contribution. Regional seismicity and stress calculations are consistent with time-dependent postseismic Coulomb stress loading of the Red River Fault, involving positive shear and extensional normal-stress changes. In the model, time-dependent lower-crustal relaxation produces postseismic stress changes comparable to the coseismic change within about a decade. Together, these observations suggest that prolonged crustal deformation, potentially reinforced by local earthquakes, contributed to the sustained far-field helium-concentration anomaly. Slip during the 2025 M7.7 Myanmar earthquake triggered high He-emissions that may persist for several decades along the Red River Fault, located around 600 km away from the epicentre, according to elevated gas-phase He concentrations in thermal-spring groundwater.

title: The ocean’s color is changing near the Great Pacific Garbage Patch
abstract:
The ocean’s color in the region of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is shifting in ways consistent with the simulated optical effects of microplastic accumulation, according to analyses of 20-year satellite records. 
 Marine microplastic pollution has proven remarkably difficult to detect from satellite. However, decades of satellite ocean color measurements have revealed long-term changes in the ocean’s optical signature, which may be influenced by the aggregation of small suspended microplastics in some regions. Analyzing three 20-year records of satellite ocean color reflectance over the North Pacific, we find distinct brightening in both blue and green spectral bands near the Great Pacific Garbage Patch relative to the surrounding ocean. Using radiative transfer modeling, we show that the spectral shift observed corresponds to expectations for the accumulation of suspended microplastics beyond reasonable uncertainty. Finally, we utilize a Monte Carlo approach to generate over 50,000 ocean brightening spectra to determine the likelihood that the observed brightening is attributable to natural multidecadal biogeochemical changes. Microplastics in the water column correspond with a more than four-fold increase in likelihood of the ocean color changes observed near the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, indicating that the spectral shape of brightening caused by small microplastics is unlikely to be caused by natural shifts in ocean color variables and may be used as a diagnostic tool to assess microplastic accumulation from satellite ocean-color measurements. The ocean’s color in the region of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is shifting in ways consistent with the simulated optical effects of microplastic accumulation, according to analyses of 20-year satellite records.

title: Microclimate persistence in island montane cloud forests
abstract:
Montane cloud forests maintain stable near-surface humidity despite regional warming, buffered by water-vapor supply, cloud-mediated cooling, and thermodynamic regulation, based on a 42-year high-resolution analysis of hourly climate data from Taiwan. 
 Montane cloud forests (MCFs), ecosystems critically dependent on persistent cloud immersion and high moisture availability, have been presumed vulnerable to regional warming and atmospheric drying. Yet their microclimatic resilience under regional climate variability remains poorly understood. Here we show that MCFs maintain remarkably stable near-surface relative humidity (RH), despite sustained regional warming, using a 42-year (1980–2021) high-resolution (2-km, hourly) climate dataset from Taiwan. These forests also exhibit substantially lower interannual RH variability than adjacent non-cloud-forested regions. This persistence arises from an interplay of mechanisms, including local and nonlocal water vapor supply under variable rainfall regimes, cloud-mediated temperature moderation, and nonlinear thermodynamic regulation. Together, these processes buffer MCFs against atmospheric drying. Our results complement prevailing assessments of MCF vulnerability to changing climate, by revealing their retention of a stable microclimate amid regional climate fluctuations. This study advances understanding of how mountain ecosystems regulate their microclimate and provides a mechanistic framework for evaluating microclimate persistence in cloud forests worldwide. title: Cascading impacts of Atlantic meridional overturning circulation weakening and collapse on marine biogeochemistry
abstract:
Atlantic meridional overturning circulation collapse would induce changes to the Earth system that may take 2-3 centuries to fully unfold, according to analyses of Earth system model ensemble simulations. 
 As Earth’s surface temperature continues to warm, the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation risks crossing a tipping point. Then, multiple Earth system components may be irreversibly altered. Here, we use the NASA-GISS Earth System Model to investigate the responses of ocean carbon uptake, net primary productivity, oxygen concentration, and carbon storage to a collapse of the overturning circulation under a moderate forcing scenario. We find that the sign of the impact in different systems is regionally-dependent, and the magnitude is generally larger in the Northern Hemisphere. We use a Least-Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator regression to provide estimates of the timescales over which these impacts begin to occur (lags) and are fully realized (latencies). Timescales are generally found to increase southward from the Northern high latitudes to the Southern Ocean, but are remarkably similar between different basins at similar latitudes. Tipping of the overturning circulation will lock-in committed changes to the Earth system that will take 2-3 centuries to fully unfold. title: Self-supervised temporal reconstruction of reanalysis fields at subhourly scales
abstract:
This article proposes a token-guided self-supervised framework that reconstructs 15-minute near-surface relative humidity and air temperature from coarse reanalysis records without high-frequency training data, providing support for fast-evolving weather events. 
 Fast-evolving weather events develop on 5–15-min timescales and can influence human activities and planning. However, most atmospheric reanalyses provide data every 1–3 h, making rapid changes difficult to capture. Traditional machine-learning approaches require high-frequency supervision labels, which limits their use when such data are unavailable. Here we present a token-guided self-supervised framework that learns temporal relationships directly from coarse archives and reconstructs subhourly fields without subhourly labels. Temporal context and the requested output time are encoded as discrete tokens and incorporated through cross-attention, enabling the model to generate intermediate states consistent with the surrounding coarse fields. Across the evaluated settings, the framework yields lower reconstruction errors than recurrent and attention-based baselines. Applied to the 1806–1900 subset of the NOAA Twentieth Century Reanalysis version 3, the framework produces 15-min ensembles of near-surface relative humidity and 2-m temperature. These reconstructions support analyses of short-term variability in historical weather records and extend event-scale analysis to periods with sparse observations. This article proposes a token-guided self-supervised framework that reconstructs 15-minute near-surface relative humidity and air temperature from coarse reanalysis records without high-frequency training data, providing support for fast-evolving weather events.

title: Reduced, fluorine-enriched mantle preconditions giant tin mineralization
abstract:
Reduced, fluorine-rich mantle conditions beneath South China may have preconditioned the crustal magmatic system for tin enrichment, providing a key deep-seated control on the formation of its world-class tin deposits, according to analysis of zircon and apatite data from Mesozoic mafic rocks across South China. 
 Mantle redox conditions and halogen budgets influence crustal ore formation, yet mantle domains beneath intraplate magmatic provinces remain poorly understood. Here we combine zircon oxybarometry and apatite halogen data from 1,515 zircon and 309 apatite grains in Mesozoic mafic rocks across South China to investigate the underlying mantle. We identify a previously unrecognized domain that produced reduced, fluorine-enriched mafic magmas. This domain lies distal to the Paleo-Pacific subduction front and coincides with the world-class South China tin province, contrasting with the more oxidized, less fluorine-enriched magmas of the continental-margin arc. We attribute this signature to metasomatic enrichment involving phlogopite-bearing assemblages. Such a mantle reservoir may precondition tin-fertile transcrustal magmatic systems by stabilizing divalent tin, suppressing tetravalent tin incorporation into early titanium-bearing minerals, and promoting tin enrichment in highly differentiated, fluorine-rich melts. These findings highlight the redox and halogen architecture of the mantle as a key deep-seated control on continental-scale tin metallogeny. title: Equivalence of pseudogap and pairing energy in a cuprate high-temperature superconductor
abstract: The pseudogap stands out in the phase diagram of the cuprate high-temperature superconductors because its origin and relationship to superconductivity remain elusive. The origin of the pseudogap has been debated, with competing hypotheses attributing it to preformed electron pairs or local order, such as charge density waves. We present unambiguous evidence supporting the pairing scenario, using local shot-noise spectroscopy measurements in Bi2Sr2CaCu2O8+δ. Our data demonstrate that the pseudogap energy coincides with the onset of electron pairing and is spatially heterogeneous with values reaching up to 70 milli–electron volts. Our results exclude a pure local order origin of the pseudogap, link the pseudogap to Cooper pair formation, and suggest that the limiting factor for higher critical temperature in cuprates is phase coherence.

title: Discovering molecular modulators with nanoswitch screening
abstract: Molecules that modulate protein-protein interactions, including through ternary complex formation, have been established as key therapeutics. Yet they can be challenging to discover, as standard screening approaches often lack throughput or fail to directly assay multibody interactions. We addressed this by combining DNA nanoswitch–based selection of nucleotide-encoded libraries with next-generation sequencing to create FIND (Functional Interaction–based Nanoswitch Discovery), which enables ultrahigh-throughput discovery of compounds that induce or increase protein-protein interactions. We demonstrate FIND by discovering nanobodies that stabilize the interaction between angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 and the receptor-binding domain of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 and by discovering agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor gamma from a DNA-barcoded small-molecule library. By enabling rapid discovery of molecular modulators, FIND could lead to new therapeutics across many conditions.

title: Tumor metastasis co-opts liver hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression
abstract: Cancer-associated hematopoietic abnormalities contribute to systemic immunosuppression. However, whether tumors can initiate localized extramedullary hematopoiesis to suppress antitumor immunity remains unclear. In this study, we identify a distinct form of hepatic hematopoiesis driven by liver metastasis–associated hematopoietic stem cells (LM-HSCs). Liver metastases establish ectopic periportal hematopoietic niches that recruit bone marrow HSCs through Kupffer cell–dependent C-C motif chemokine receptor 1 (CCR1) signaling. Although LM-HSCs retain self-renewal and multipotency, cAMP response element–binding protein (CREB) activation skews their differentiation toward the myeloid lineage, particularly annexin A1–positive (ANXA1+) immature neutrophils. These neutrophils produce glucocorticoids, which activate glucocorticoid receptor signaling in a paracrine manner and induce immune checkpoint receptor expression and functional anergy in CD8+T and natural killer cells. Collectively, these findings suggest that liver metastases reprograms hepatic hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression.
